Q: Checking if a graph is connected with Z3 A:

You could check graph connectivity by something like this:

from z3 import *

solver = Solver()

nodes = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F", "G"]
Nodes = range(len(nodes))

edges = [ ["A", "B", 5], ["B", "C", 1], ["C", "D", 7], ["D", "A", 9], ["E", "F", 3], ["F", "G", 2], ["G", "E", 3]]

''' every node has a level '''
levels = [Int(f'L{nd}') for nd in Nodes]

''' first node has level 0 '''
solver.add(levels[0] == 0)

''' all nodes != root must have a level one higher than a neighbor node '''
for nd in Nodes:
    if nd > 0:
        ''' collect a set of neighbor nodes connected to node nd '''
        print(f'Node {nd} {nodes[nd]}')
        neighbors = set([nodes.index(x) for x, y, _ in edges if y == nodes[nd]]+[nodes.index(y) for x, y, _ in edges if x == nodes[nd]])
        print(f'neighbors {neighbors}')
        ''' at least one neighbor node must have a level one below '''
        solver.add(Or([levels[nd] == (levels[n] + 1) for n in neighbors]))

if solver.check() == sat:
    print("Graph is connected")
else:
    print("Graph is not connected")

Q: How can I get the date of the first day of a year? A:

You can use following ways:

1)
Use make_date function

make_date(year, month, day)

https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/functions/date

To get first day of the year (returns a date type):

SELECT make_date(year(today()), 1, 1);

Use date_trunc function:

To get first day of the year (returns a date type):

SELECT date_trunc('year', today());

Example outputs (using https://shell.duckdb.org/):

duckdb> select make_date(year(today()), 1, 1);
┌──────────────────────────────────┐
│ make_date("year"(today()), 1, 1) │
╞══════════════════════════════════╡
│ 2026-01-01                       │
└──────────────────────────────────┘

duckdb> select typeof(make_date(year(today()), 1, 1));
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ typeof(make_date("year"(today()), 1, 1)) │
╞══════════════════════════════════════════╡
│ DATE                                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘

duckdb> select date_trunc('year', today());
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ date_trunc('year', today()) │
╞═════════════════════════════╡
│ 2026-01-01                  │
└─────────────────────────────┘

duckdb> select typeof(date_trunc('year', today()));
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│ typeof(date_trunc('year', today())) │
╞═════════════════════════════════════╡
│ DATE                                │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘

Q: `reinterpret_cast` between unrelated structs A:

The Standard specifies that a reinterpret_cast between object pointers is the equivalent of a double static_cast from A* to void* and then to B* ([expr.reinterpret.cast]/7). The formal rule for when this is blessed by the Standard is in [basic.compound]/4 (some minor formating changes):

Two objects a and b are pointer-interconvertible if:

  1. they are the same object, or
  2. one is a union object and the other is a non-static data member of that object, or
  3. one is a standard-layout class object and the other is the first non-static data member of that object or any base class subobject of that object, or
  4. there exists an object c such that a and c are pointer-interconvertible, and c and b are pointer-interconvertible.

If two objects are pointer-interconvertible, then they have the same address, and it is possible to obtain a pointer to one from a pointer to the other via a reinterpret_cast.

Unrelated structs that happen to have compatible object representations do not meet any of these conditions, but a reinterpret_cast between correctly-aligned pointers to the two types will often work anyway. In fact, the C++ Core Guidelines even recommend that, if you must type-pun, do it this way.¹

Most exceptions involve the Strict-Aliasing Rule, which gives compilers license to assume that an A* and a B* can never alias the same object and break the program in arbitrary ways if they ever do (except for a few special cases such as void*, char* and unsigned char*, which can alias anything). There could be a standard-conforming implementation where this fails completely, though, even with no aliasing. For example, the runtime is allowed to keep track of which objects it created where, and crash if the program attempts to access a memory address through an incompatible pointer. It’s even plausible to me that an implementation designed for memory safety would.

One standard way to do this is to make each struct (which must be a C-like “standard-layout struct,” not something complex like an object with virtual functions or inheritance) a member of the same union. If the first member or members members of different structs in the union are layout-compatible, you can then type-pun on those members by reading the fields of the other union member. To quote the Standard ([class.union.general], note 1):

One special guarantee is made in order to simplify the use of unions: If a standard-layout union contains several standard-layout structs that share a common initial sequence, and if a non-static data member of an object of this standard-layout union type is active and is one of the standard-layout structs, it is permitted to inspect the common initial sequence of any of the standard-layout struct members

The formal definition of “common initial sequence” is in [class.mem.general]/23, but it basically means a sequence of members at the beginning of both structs that have the same types in the same order. So for example,

    union {
        A a = {.x = 1, .y = 2.0f, .z = 3.0, .arr = {}};
        B b;
    }; // Type-pun from A to B through an anonymous union.

    std::cout << b.x << ' ' << b.y << ' ' << b.z << '\n';

If the structures can be type-punned by copying their object representations with memcpy(), you can also convert from one to the other using std::bit_cast. If the source object is correctly-aligned for the type you want to convert to, std::start_lifetime_as is how you replace an object with a new object of a different type, at the same memory location, with the same object representation. (This does not let you break the Strict-Aliasing Rule: the original object that was there is replaced.) See [obj.lifetime]. Unless you are dealing with padding bits, invalid value representations or misaligned pointers, these conversions do not have undefined behavior. ([bit.cast])

¹ This guideline is obsolete in modern C++. Use either std::bit_cast or std::start_lieftime_as instead.

Q: Convert weston-calibrator values to LIBINPUT_CALIBRATION_MATRIX A:

It looks like the main issue is the difference in how Weston and libinput interpret the calibration coordinates, especially with respect to device resolution scaling. In my experience, treating the width and height as “1” essentially normalizes the values, but the placement in the 3x3 matrix can be tricky to get right. Some people find it helps to average multiple runs and carefully map the offsets to the translation components. Out of curiosity, have you tried testing smaller incremental adjustments to see if the touchscreen starts registering partial touches, similar to how sallimoservice fine-tunes timing and routes for precision?

Q: Python cast byte array to C void pointer A:

ctypes.cast() does not work directly on bytearray because bytearray is not a ctypes object. cast() expects either a ctypes instance or something that already exposes a compatible C representation.

Instead of casting the bytearray itself, you should obtain a pointer to its underlying buffer using ctypes utilities.

import ctypes

buf = bytearray(16)
ptr = ctypes.c_void_p(ctypes.addressof(
    (ctypes.c_char * len(buf)).from_buffer(buf)
))

print(ptr)

Q: How can we include a verbatim cli table in a cli_warn() message? A:

cli_warn uses cli_bullets to format the paramater message which likely messes up your cli-table. A hacky approach could be to replace spaces " " with non-break spaces. Printing a table inside a warning is limited by getOption(warning.length)

warning.length: sets the truncation limit in bytes for error and warning messages. A non-negative integer, with allowed values 100...8170, default 1000.

I guess you can tackle that limitation by splitting the table and throwing multiple warnings. But this approach works and the warnings can be suppressed.

library(dplyr)
library(cli)
library(clitable)

check_complete <- function(data, cols) {
  missing <- data |>
    dplyr::select({{cols}}) |>
    dplyr::filter(if_any(dplyr::everything(), ~ is.na(.)))
  
  nrow_missing <- nrow(missing)
  
  if(nrow_missing > 0){
    table_text <- cli_table(missing)
    old <- options(warning.length = 8170)
    on.exit(options(old), add = TRUE)
    # include the table in the warning message
    cli_warn(c("There are {nrow_missing} rows with missing values in the specified columns:",
               gsub(" ", "\u00a0", table_text)))
  }
}
data(starwars, package = "dplyr")

suppressMessages(check_complete(dplyr::bind_rows(replicate(10, starwars, simplify = FALSE)), c(name:hair_color)))

# Warning:
#  There are 330 rows with missing values in the specified columns:
# ┌─────────────────────┬──────┬────┬────────────┐
# │ name                │height│mass│ hair_color │
# ├─────────────────────┼──────┼────┼────────────┤
# │ C-3PO               │ 167  │  75│ NA         │
# │ R2-D2               │  96  │  32│ NA         │
# │ R5-D4               │  97  │  32│ NA         │
# │ Wilhuff Tarkin      │ 180  │ NA │auburn, grey│
# │ Greedo              │ 173  │  74│ NA         │
# │Jabba Desilijic Tiure│ 175  │1358│ NA         │
# │ Mon Mothma          │ 150  │ NA │ auburn     │
# │ Arvel Crynyd        │ NA   │ NA │ brown      │

# ... I cut the output here. The table continues until maximum of 8170 byte chars is hit

If you capture this warning log with sink or similar, there might be oddities searching the string for "C-3PO ", if there is actually "\u00a0" instead of " ". But if it's just about a visual table within a warning message, this might work for you. For large tables this will be slow. You can consider cutting off the table before warning

table_text <- cli_table(missing[1:min(100, nrow(missing)),])

and

"There are {nrow_missing} rows with missing values in the specified columns. Showing a maximum of first 100 rows:
